new_statements.quote: Azeri word accent follows general Turkic patterns. There is normally a high pitch on the last syllable and often an expiratory stress on the first one. Some suffixes, e.g. personal markers of pronominal origin and the negation suffix, move the accent to the syllable preceding them. The melodious sentence intonation is influenced by Persian and sounds rather different ...

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (StressTyp2 final stress = final stress); adds that the final prominence is a high pitch, that an expiratory stress often sits on the first syllable, and that pronominal personal markers and the negation suffix are pre-accenting. CAUTION on provenance: the listed open_url (the Harvard library catalogue record cdi_proquest_journals_2915116240) is the WRONG ITEM: its PNX metadata identifies it as Ragagnin 2022, 'Ostensive markers in Azeri and some other Turkic languages', Turkic Languages 26(2): 67-80 (open access at iris.unive.it). I downloaded and read that paper in full (, 14 pp.): it has no phonology section and zero hits for stress/accent/prosody/pitc…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent is on the last syllable (realised as high pitch), with a frequent additional expiratory (dynamic) stress on the first syllable; a set of unstressable suffixes (pronominal-origin personal markers, the negation suffix -mA) push the accent onto the syllable before them.
new_statements.secondary_stress: An expiratory stress 'often' on the first syllable alongside the final high pitch; the work does not call it secondary stress, but it amounts to initial secondary prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: Pre-accenting suffixes: personal markers of pronominal origin and the negation suffix move the accent to the preceding syllable.
new_statements.identity_note: The chapter describes Azeri in general (Northern/Republic standard and, per the intonation remark, Persian-influenced varieties); the wrong-item 2022 paper focuses on Northern Azeri, the official language of Azerbaijan. No dialect-specific stress claim was found.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim in the Cambridge PDF we hold at p.211 'Prosodic features' (p.5). (2) Deciding source is a 2017 JIPA Illustration — a peer-reviewed phonetic description — but of the Tabriz (Iranian) variety, which Glottolog files under South Azerbaijani (sout2697); StressTyp2's Householder & Lotfi 1965 is Tabriz-based too (ERIC record). The catalog has no separate sout2697 record, so this is not a duplicate, and the held North-Azerbaijani academy sketch (Širaliev 1997:162 §2.1.2, Baku standard) independently states final stress in native words with unstressed predicative/negation affixes and source-stress in Russian loans — the same system. The newly downloaded UT Austin course (North Azerbaijani, 2006) also confirms. Coding fixed-strict final is consistent with every other Turkic record in the catalog. sources.citation: Essentials of Azerbaijani: An Introductory Course. University of Texas at Austin (Dept. of Slavic and Eurasian Studies), PDF dated 2006, 127 pp; no author on title page.
sources.quote: 'The majority of words in Azerbaijani are stressed on the last syllable. In this course, for words or word forms where the stress is not on the final syllable, an accent mark will be written over the stressed vowel.' ... 'In most cases, the stress in an Azerbaijani word will shift to the final syllable of an added suffix' ... personal verbal suffixes of 'to be' 'are not stressed'; 'proféssor'-type loans keep non-final stress under suffixation.
sources.locator: p.13, Introduction 'The Sounds of Azerbaijani'; also catalog record (plural suffix takes stress), catalog record 'A note about stress' (copular personal suffixes unstressed), negative -mA shifts stress left
